decisions.reason: Konowal et al. (2026) evaluate an organizational behavior management (OBM) supervisor training and dresser job-aid intervention for direct service providers (DSPs) across five residential students with autism and intellectual disability ('A Five-Case Replication Series') to address parent complaints that students wore other students' clothing rather than their own personal clothing. While the Introduction reviews three prior clothing-related studies—Nutter and Reid (1978), McClannahan et al. (1990), and Buckley et al. (2025) (which evaluated a care-provider checklist and visual-cue intervention for general clothing appearance and personal hygiene)—and notes that 'Like McClannahan et al. (1990) and Buckley et al. (2025), the present five-case replication series did not focus directly on teaching students dressing skills, rather evaluated the effects of training care providers to monitor and assist the students wearing personal clothing,' the authors explicitly state that their objective was 'to evaluate the effectiveness of training on a facet of clothing appearance not studied previously' and reiterate in Treatment Implications that 'evaluation of procedures to overcome these problems has not been researched previously.' The 'five-case replication series' refers to repeating the intervention across five students within this study, not empirically retesting Buckley et al. (2025); thus, under the Codebook, type is not_a_replication.
